SECURITY ENGINEERING ANSWER — NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts)

BOTTOM LINE. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 prescribes no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no time window in which those attempts are counted, and no lockout duration. All three are organization-defined parameters (ODPs). The published control is a template; the implementing organization supplies the values in its security plan. Any document that quotes a concrete attempt count, window or lockout duration as 'the AC-7 requirement' is quoting a local parameter assignment, not NIST.

1. THE CONTROL AS PUBLISHED (verbatim, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC family, sha256 fc63bcd61715):

"AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS
Control:
a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded."

2. WHERE EACH OF THE THREE ASKED-FOR VALUES LIVES, AND WHAT NIST SAYS ABOUT IT.

  Ask 1 — number of consecutive invalid logon attempts
    Location: AC-7a, first parameter.
    Control notation: "[Assignment: organization-defined number]".
    What NIST states: no figure. The number is an assignment the organization makes.
    Status: answered as a verdict (organization-defined); see results entry 1.

  Ask 2 — time period within which the attempts are counted
    Location: AC-7a, second parameter.
    Control notation: "[Assignment: organization-defined time period]".
    What NIST states: no figure. The window is an assignment the organization makes.
    Status: the page states none — see not_stated entry 2 and section 5.

  Ask 3 — lockout duration
    Location: AC-7b, first option of the Selection, i.e. "lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]".
    Control notation: an organization-defined time period nested inside a Selection option.
    What NIST states: no figure. Two additional qualifications matter:
      (i) The duration only exists if the organization selects that option. AC-7b is a Selection (one or more): lock for an organization-defined period, lock until released by an administrator, delay the next logon prompt per an organization-defined delay algorithm, notify the system administrator, or take another organization-defined action. An implementation that satisfies (b) by delay-and-notify has no lockout duration at all and is still conformant.
      (ii) The control's own discussion warns against permanent lockout: "Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period." The word 'usually' means even the auto-release behaviour is a design choice, not a prescribed duration.
    Status: the page states none — see not_stated entry 3 and section 5.

3. THE PARAMETERIZATION MODEL — WHY THERE IS NO NUMBER TO FIND.

Bracketed text in Rev. 5 is not prose to be read past; it is the control's parameter interface. "[Assignment: ...]" marks an organization-defined parameter (ODP) that the organization must fill; "[Selection (one or more): ...]" marks a choice set from which the organization must select. AC-7 therefore has, at minimum, three assignable values and one selection, and the values are set per organization (and, where justified, per system) in the SSP. The Rev. 4-to-5 comparison workbook (sha256 94465ffc5584) records the change explicitly for AC-7: "Changes control text / Changes parameter / Changes discussion — Parameter includes additional selection options when the number of allowed consecutive invalid logon attempts threshold is exceeded." So Rev. 5 widened the choice set in (b); it did not add a number.

Baseline applicability does not add values either. Table D-1 (Control Baselines) lists "AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts — AC-7 AC-7 AC-7" across the Low, Moderate and High columns: the control is required at every impact level, but the baseline entry names the control, not its parameter values.

Related requirements in the same control family, for completeness — every one of them is likewise organization-defined and none supplies a figure that could be borrowed for AC-7:
  - AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lock — "[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]" (the r4-to-r5 workbook notes it was "Previously withdrawn in Rev4; Incorporated into AC-7").
  - AC-7(2) Purge or Wipe Mobile Device — wipe "after [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts".
  - AC-7(3) Biometric Attempt Limiting — "Limit the number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Assignment: organization-defined number]."
  - AC-7(4) Use of Alternate Authentication Factor — "(b) Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts through use of the alternative factors by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]."

4. WHAT THE SECURITY ENGINEER MUST PRODUCE INSTEAD OF A NUMBER.

Because the values are ours to set, the deliverable for a system is a documented, defensible ODP assignment plus the configuration that implements it. Procedure:

  Step 1 — Open a parameter record for AC-7 in the SSP with three assignment fields (attempt count; counting window; lockout period) and one selection field (which AC-7b actions are implemented). Give each field an owner, a value, a rationale, and a source-of-decision (policy, risk assessment, or authorizing official direction).

  Step 2 — Decide AC-7b's selection BEFORE the lockout period, because the period is only meaningful if the 'lock the account or node for an organization-defined time period' option is chosen. Record every selected action; the control permits one or more.

  Step 3 — Justify the three assignments against the two opposing risks the control names. Brute-force/credential-stuffing exposure pushes the attempt count and window down and the lockout up; denial-of-service against legitimate users (including the help-desk cost of unlocks) pushes them the other way. State the reasoning in the SSP — an assessor will test the assignment against its stated rationale, not against a NIST number, because no NIST number exists.

  Step 4 — Specify the implementation precisely enough to test: where the counter lives (per account, per source address, per credential), what resets it (the control's own discussion of AC-7(2) establishes the principle that a successful logon resets the count), what happens at the threshold, who can release a lock, whether AC-7(4) alternate factors provide a bypass path, how lockouts are logged and alerted, and — where AC-7(2)/(3) are selected — the mobile-device wipe threshold and the biometric attempt limit as separate ODPs.

  Step 5 — Collect assessment evidence: the SSP parameter record, the actual account-lockout configuration from the authenticating component (operating system and application layers both, since the discussion notes responses may be implemented at both), and a test showing the threshold, the window and the release behaviour match the recorded assignment.

5. EVIDENCE THAT NIST STATES NO FIGURE (what was searched, and where).

  Ask 2: full text of the Rev. 5 draft baseline-markup pages (https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/ipd/docs/sp800-53r5-draft-baselines-markup.pdf and its identical mirror under csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/publications/..., 10 pages, 19,808 characters, sha256 bba84ffcac41) contains none of 'time period', 'specified period of time', 'period of time', 'time period specified by the organization'. No counting window is stated.

  Ask 3: full text of NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf, 492 pages, 1,561,656 characters, sha256 fc63bcd61715), the OSCAL-derived Rev. 5.1 (396 pages, sha256 9ce01f4d67c9), the AC-7 wiki page (122,491 characters, sha256 080f4279d095), the bsafes mirror (17,836 characters, sha256 f9630cd5ebc4), the Rev. 5 draft (481 pages, sha256 d1fd2107db9d), the Rev. 5 draft controls markup (282 pages, sha256 8574eeabc495), the csrc Rev. 5 draft (494 pages, sha256 bdca6784056e), both baseline-markup drafts, and the r4-to-r5 comparison workbook (262,589 characters, sha256 94465ffc5584) contains none of 'lockout duration', 'account lockout duration', 'time period the account is locked', 'lockout time period'. No lockout duration is stated. Note the distinction: the concept of a lock period is present in AC-7b, but only as the placeholder '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]'; the document states no duration.

  Ask 1 carries no proof of absence, so it is not reported as 'none stated'; it is answered on the control text itself, which assigns the number to the organization.

6. SCOPE DISCIPLINE — WHAT NOT TO CITE AS THE AC-7 ANSWER.

  - NIST SP 800-63B addresses authenticator throttling and rate limiting. It is a different document with a different scope (digital identity), it is not AC-7, and no figure from it appears in the evidence gathered here — so none is reproduced in this answer. If a program wants to adopt a 800-63B figure, that is a deliberate crosswalk decision and must be cited to 800-63B, not to 800-53.
  - Vendor defaults, CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs and OS group-policy defaults all supply concrete numbers. Each is a legitimate source for an organizational ODP assignment, and each should be cited as such in the SSP rationale — never as 'what NIST requires'.
  - Rev. 4 wording differs from Rev. 5 (Rev. 5 added the 'notify system administrator' and 'take other action' options to AC-7b). Quoting a Rev. 4 sentence as current is an error; the Rev. 5 text is the one reproduced in section 1.

7. PROVENANCE. All control text quoted above is from NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf, sha256 fc63bcd61715) and corroborated on the OSCAL-derived Rev. 5.1 PDF (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9), the AC-7 wiki page (sha256 080f4279d095) and the bsafes mirror (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4), all of which carry identical control wording. Baseline placement is from Table D-1 of the draft baseline markup (sha256 bba84ffcac41). The Rev. 4-to-5 change note is from the r4-to-r5 comparison workbook (sha256 94465ffc5584).

# NASA-STD-4003A — Class R (EMI/RF) Bond: What the Standard Actually Requires

## 0. Bottom line

**NASA-STD-4003A does not specify a maximum RF impedance in ohms at any stated frequency for a Class R bond joint. There is no number to look up, and no test frequency to cite.** The standard imposes exactly two things on a Class R joint:

1. **A performance requirement (no number, no frequency).** 4.1.4b [EBR 21]: *“All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.”*
2. **One numeric per-joint constraint, and it is dc, not RF.** 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]: *“The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.”*

The standard's own rationale (Appendix A.3.4) removes any doubt that 2.5 mΩ is meant as an RF figure: *“There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent… The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.”* And: *“The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.”*

So the answer to the designer is: **comply with ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc per joint, and separately prove — by analysis, at your program's frequencies of interest — that the joint impedance is low enough not to cause interference. The standard will not give you an ohm figure; your EMC control plan must.**

---

## 1. Verbatim requirement text (NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1; identical Class R text in base 4003A §4.1.4)

| Ref | Requirement (as published) |

| 4.1.4a [EBR 20] | “All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.” |
| 4.1.4b [EBR 21] | “All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.” |
| 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] | “The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.” |
| 4.1.4c [EBR 23] | “The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.” |
| 4.1.4d [EBR 24] | “Hatches, access panels, doors, and other apertures in outer mold line components shall have at minimum a Class R electrical bond to the outer mold line material.” |
| 4.1.4.1 [EBR 27] | “The dc resistance for each joint in the backshell-to-case path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.” |
| Table 1, Class R column | DC BOND RESISTANCE REQMT: “Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.” FREQ. REQMT: **High**. CURRENT REQMT: **Low**. Qualitative note: “Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.” |
| Verification section | “Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection.” / “The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds.” / “The resistance of bonds may be measured on flight vehicles, but it is usually impractical to measure inductance or current carrying capability.” |
| Appendix A.3.4 (rationale) | “The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation…, the area of the faying surfaces in contact, and the amount of pressure holding the surfaces together… The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.” / “RF bonds may be satisfactory with several ohms of impedance; but, when straps are used, even these levels will be quickly exceeded as frequency increases.” / “Any electronic equipment with conductive mounting feet will probably have an inductive reactance greater than 2.5 milliohms at frequencies above 10 megahertz (MHz).” |

Note the requirement architecture: **4.1.4b is the requirement; 4.1.4b(1) is a sub-requirement that is necessary but not sufficient.** Passing 2.5 mΩ dc does not discharge 4.1.4b.

---

## 2. Why there is no “ohms at X MHz” figure — and why you should stop looking for one

- **The requirement is written as an outcome, not a limit.** “Low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest” is a tailoring instruction to the program. The frequencies of interest are defined by the vehicle's emitter/receiver set and the equipment's emission/susceptibility profile — not by the bonding standard. 4003A cannot know your band, so it cannot give your limit.
- **No RF impedance measurement is defined.** 4003A defines a dc resistance verification (sample bond testing) and requires Class R to be verified by *analysis and inspection*. There is no RF bridge / network-analyzer procedure, no test electrode geometry, and no test frequency in the document.
- **The standard's own appendix contradicts a numeric RF reading of 2.5 mΩ.** It says the value has “no RF design basis,” that acceptable RF impedance “may be in the ohms range,” and that a dc-compliant joint can still be RF-poor.
- **Revision check.** The base NASA-STD-4003A is filed as “Historical” relative to **NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1** (revalidated 03-13-2026), which is the current issue and carries the [EBR nn] requirement tags used above. The Class R technical content is unchanged between the two. Confirm at time of use that no 4003B has superseded it.

**If a contract or a reviewer demands “the number,” the honest answer is: 4003A does not contain one; the number must be generated by the program's EMC control plan (or invoked from a cited alternate standard), and recorded as a tailored requirement.**

---

## 3. The one numeric constraint, precisely scoped

**2.5 milliohms, dc, across *each joint* in the Class R path — not across the whole path.**

- “Joint” = a single faying interface (equipment foot to bracket, bracket to deck, connector backshell to case, panel to OML skin). The standard's own worked illustration: *“A realistic value would be on the order of 10 milliohms from the shield to the electronics enclosure for a cadmium-plated aluminum assembly, with 2.5 milliohms maximum for any particular joint.”* So a three-joint path may legitimately read ~7.5 mΩ end-to-end while every joint is compliant.
- Measurement is a dc four-wire (Kelvin) resistance with probes straddling the joint interface, hardware in flight configuration, surfaces at flight finish. Record per joint, not per path.
- The requirement is repeated verbatim for the shield-termination path (4.1.4.1 [EBR 27], backshell-to-case).
- **Nothing in the standard caps RF impedance in ohms. The 2.5 mΩ is the ceiling on the resistive term only.**

---

## 4. Why 2.5 mΩ dc tells you almost nothing about RF — worked numbers

For a bond, Z(f) is dominated by inductance above a few tens of kHz. Estimate a strap as a rectangular bar:

  L ≈ (μ0·l / 2π) · [ ln( 2l/(w+t) ) + 0.5 + (w+t)/(3l) ]   (l, w, t in metres; μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m)

This is a free-space estimate; mounted close to structure the measured value is typically 20–50 % lower. It is an estimate — validate by measurement or full-wave simulation for critical joints.

| Strap | l × w × t (mm) | L (nH) | XL @1 MHz | @10 MHz | @30 MHz | @100 MHz | @400 MHz | f where XL = 2.5 mΩ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 25 × 12.7 × 1 | 9.9 | 62 mΩ | 0.62 Ω | 1.87 Ω | 6.2 Ω | 24.9 Ω | 40 kHz |
| B | 12 × 25 × 1 | 2.7 | 17 mΩ | 0.17 Ω | 0.51 Ω | 1.70 Ω | 6.8 Ω | 145 kHz |
| C | 50 × 12.7 × 1 | 25.8 | 162 mΩ | 1.62 Ω | 4.86 Ω | 16.2 Ω | 64.8 Ω | 15.4 kHz |

(XL = 2πfL; crossover f = 0.0025 / (2πL).)

**Read the last column.** For ordinary strap geometries, the inductive reactance exceeds the 2.5 mΩ dc limit somewhere between 15 kHz and 150 kHz. Above that, the dc measurement is measuring a term that no longer governs. Strap C is at 1 Ω by 6 MHz — exactly the behaviour 4003A warns about (“when straps are used, even these levels will be quickly exceeded as frequency increases”).

**And the resonance clause is not decorative.** Model a joint as R–L in series, shunted by the small capacitance across the interface. Take L = 9.9 nH (strap A), C = 2 pF, R = 2.5 mΩ:

- f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(9.9×10⁻⁹ × 2×10⁻¹²)) ≈ **1.13 GHz**
- Q = ω_r L / R ≈ 2π(1.13×10⁹)(9.9×10⁻⁹)/0.0025 ≈ 2.8×10⁴
- Z_peak ≈ L/(R·C) = 9.9×10⁻⁹/(2.5×10⁻³ × 2×10⁻¹²) ≈ **2×10⁶ Ω**

A joint that passes 2.5 mΩ dc with margin can present megohms at ~1 GHz. That is precisely why 4.1.4b says “including resonances,” and why a dc-only compliance argument is indefensible for a Class R joint.

---

## 5. Procedure: how to produce the number 4003A does not give you

**Step 1 — Fix the frequencies of interest.** From the EMC control plan: every emitter on the vehicle (transmitters, clock harmonics, switching converters, digital edge rates), and every victim's susceptibility band. Take the *highest* significant frequency f_hi and the band(s) where a resonance could fall. State them explicitly — this is the “stated frequency” the standard refuses to supply.

**Step 2 — Derive the allowable joint impedance.**

  Z_max(f) = V_allow(f) / I_noise(f)

where I_noise is the worst-case RF current driven through the bond path (structure current from an illuminated vehicle, shield current on a terminated cable, or the enclosure current of the emitting equipment) and V_allow is the interference voltage the victim can tolerate with margin. Both come from the EMC control plan, not from 4003A.

**Step 3 — Convert to an inductance budget.** Above the R-dominant region, L_max = Z_max / (2πf). Check that the budget is not violated at f_r of the chosen geometry.

**Step 4 — Select the joint construction** (direct lap joint vs. strap) against that budget — see §6.

**Step 5 — Verify by analysis + inspection (Class R), and by test (dc resistance).** See §7.

### Worked example (illustrative — program-derived, NOT a 4003A requirement)

- f_hi = 400 MHz (co-located UHF transmitter + digital edge rates).
- Worst-case structure current coupled through the bond: I = 50 mA.
- Allowable interference voltage at the enclosure: V = 25 mV.
- Z_max = 0.025 / 0.05 = **0.5 Ω at 400 MHz**.
- L_max = 0.5 / (2π × 4×10⁸) = **0.20 nH**.

Conclusion from the budget: **no discrete strap can meet 0.2 nH** (best strap in the table is 2.7 nH, ~13× over). The joint must be a **direct metal-to-metal lap joint with large overlap** — e.g. 25 mm × 25 mm minimum overlap, ≥4 fasteners on ≤25 mm centres, conductive finish per the drawing, no jumper. First-order parallel-plate estimate for that overlap (l = w = 25 mm, bondline h = 0.1 mm): L ≈ μ0·h·l/w ≈ 0.13 nH, i.e. inside budget before fastener contributions — which is exactly why 4003A says “Direct contact preferred. No jumpers.”

Repeat at 30 MHz with the same currents: Z_max = 0.5 Ω → L_max = 0.5/(2π×3×10⁷) = **2.65 nH** → strap B (2.74 nH) is marginal, strap A (9.9 nH) fails, direct contact passes comfortably. **The same bond can pass at HF and fail at UHF; the standard's silence on frequency is not an oversight, it is the tailoring hook.**

---

## 6. Construction guidance the standard (and its cited rationale) does support

1. **Direct faying-surface contact first.** 4003A Table 1: “Direct contact preferred.” Appendix A.3.4: impedance depends on surface preparation, faying-surface area, and contact pressure — so specify finish, contact area, and torque, and put them on the drawing.
2. **No jumpers. No pigtails.** Table 1: “No jumpers.” Shield terminations must be 360° peripheral (4.1.4.1).
3. **Straps are a last resort and must be short and wide.** “Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.” NASA's companion EMC design-practice guidance (NTRS 19970005154, §C.2.3.5.3) gives the rule of thumb: **strap length-to-width ratio ≤ 5:1**. A 25 mm-long strap should be ≥5 mm wide; wider is better — see the table in §4, where doubling width and halving length cuts L by ~3.6×.
4. **Parallel paths, not bigger single paths.** Inductance falls with parallel current paths far faster than with added cross-section, because skin depth already forces current to the surface.
5. **Avoid the parallel resonance.** Either keep the joint loop area (hence L) low so f_r is above the band of interest, or damp it. Never let f_r land inside a receiver band or an emitter band.
6. **OML and apertures are Class R by default** (4.1.4c, 4.1.4d) — hatches, doors, and access panels are bond joints and must be analysed as such, with EMI gasketing where the joint cannot be made continuous.
7. **Multi-purpose bonds take the union of the requirements.** 4003A: an avionics unit needing both Class R (RF) and Class H (fault current) must be “low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R” *and* have contact area adequate for the maximum fault current.

---

## 7. Verification and compliance evidence package

| Requirement | Method per 4003A | Evidence to produce |
|---|---|---|
| 4.1.4b [EBR 21] impedance low enough at frequencies of interest | **Analysis + inspection** (“Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection”) | Per-joint Z(f) analysis: R_dc measured, L computed/measured, C estimated, swept 0 Hz → f_hi (and beyond f_r). Plot Z vs f against the program's Z_max(f) budget. Include resonance check. |
| 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc per joint | **Test** (“The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds”; flight-vehicle resistance measurement permitted) | Bond log: joint ID, drawing zone, finish, four-wire dc resistance, test current, date, operator. Per joint, not per path. |
| 4.1.4a/c/d [EBR 20/23/24] configuration | **Inspection** | Installation drawing call-outs: finishes, contact area, fastener torque, strap length:width ≤ 5:1, no jumpers, 360° shield termination. |
| 4.1.4.1 [EBR 27] backshell-to-case ≤ 2.5 mΩ | Test + inspection | Connector build records. |

**Measurement notes.** Four-wire Kelvin, probes straddling the joint interface only (not the strap), hardware at flight torque, ≥1 A test current, both surfaces at flight finish. Do not accept an end-to-end path reading as evidence for a joint; do not accept a joint reading as evidence for the path.

**Do not claim RF compliance from a dc measurement.** 4003A Appendix A.3.4 explicitly forecloses that argument; a reviewer who knows the standard will reject it.

---

## 8. Common errors this question usually contains

| Assumption | What 4003A actually says |
|---|---|
| “Class R has an RF impedance limit of X ohms at Y MHz.” | No such limit, no such frequency. 4.1.4b is performance-based. |
| “2.5 mΩ is the RF impedance limit.” | 2.5 mΩ is **dc resistance across each joint** (4.1.4b(1)). |
| “It measures 2.5 mΩ dc, so the RF bond is good.” | Explicitly denied in Appendix A.3.4. |
| “There must be an RF impedance test in the standard.” | No RF impedance measurement is defined; Class R is verified by analysis and inspection. |
| “Straps are acceptable for Class R.” | “No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.” |
| “2.5 mΩ applies to the whole path.” | It applies to **each joint** in the path; the path may legitimately read higher. |

---

## 9. Benchmark values from other documents — reference only, NOT 4003A requirements

If the program must cite a numeric RF impedance because its own EMC plan is silent, these are the numbers that exist in the literature, and they must be invoked **by name**, not attributed to 4003A:

- **MIL-STD-1310G:** < 25 Ω at 30 MHz for all electronic equipment to structure.
- **SSP-30245 (ISS):** < 100 mΩ at 1 MHz, excluding strap impedance.
- **MIL-B-5087B / MIL-STD-464:** 2.5 mΩ dc across each joint (Navy/Army aircraft wording).
- **NASA-STD-4003A:** *no RF impedance figure at all* — only the qualitative 4.1.4b requirement and the 2.5 mΩ dc per-joint limit.

---

## 10. Traceability

| Statement | Source |
|---|---|
| Class R definition, 2.5 mΩ, low inductance, high-frequency requirement, “direct contact preferred / no jumpers” | NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, Table 1 (Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes) and §4.1.4 |
| 4.1.4a–d requirement text, [EBR 20]–[EBR 24] | NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, §4.1.4 |
| 2.5 mΩ dc per joint, [EBR 22] | §4.1.4b(1) |
| 2.5 mΩ backshell-to-case, [EBR 27] | §4.1.4.1 |
| “No RF design basis,” “ohms range for RF,” “resistance is overshadowed by inductive reactance,” resonance behaviour, 20 dB/decade, mounting feet > 2.5 mΩ above 10 MHz | NASA-STD-4003A Appendix A.3.4 |
| “Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection”; sample-bond resistance testing; impracticality of flight inductance measurement | NASA-STD-4003A verification section |
| Strap length:width ≤ 5:1 rule of thumb | NASA NTRS 19970005154, §C.2.3.5.3 (companion EMC design guidance) |
| MIL-STD-1310G 25 Ω @ 30 MHz; SSP-30245 100 mΩ @ 1 MHz; MIL-STD-464 2.5 mΩ dc | NASA NTRS 19980201283, survey of bonding standards (secondary source) |

---

## 11. One-paragraph answer to hand the designer

NASA-STD-4003A does not give a maximum RF impedance in ohms at any frequency for a Class R bond joint. It requires (4.1.4b) that the bond path and every joint in it be designed so that inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest, and it caps the dc resistance across each joint at 2.5 milliohms (4.1.4b(1)); the backshell-to-case path carries the same 2.5 mΩ per-joint cap (4.1.4.1). CHILLER CAPACITY — 10 TONS OF REFRIGERATION TO kW (NIST SP 811)

ANSWER
  Capacity = 35.17 kW (thermal, heat-removal rate) to four significant figures.
  (= 35 170 W = 0.03517 MW; unrounded 35.1685 kW)

1. GOVERNING DEFINITION AND OFFICIAL NIST FACTOR

The ton of refrigeration is defined as 12 000 Btu_IT per hour, where Btu_IT is the International Table British thermal unit. NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 Edition, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)), Appendix B, Conversion Factors, table "Heat Flow Rate," publishes verbatim:

    ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT/h)   watt (W)   3.516 853 E+03

NIST Special Publication 1038 (The International System of Units (SI) — Conversion Factors for General Use) publishes the same factor already expressed in kilowatts:

    ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)   kilowatt (kW)   3.516 853

Both are the same official NIST factor, 3.516 853 kW per ton of refrigeration. The factor is exact in principle (12 000 Btu_IT/h is an exact definition and the Btu_IT-to-joule relation is exact); NIST prints it to seven significant figures.

2. COMPUTATION — THREE INDEPENDENT ROUTES

Route A — direct NIST kW factor (SP 1038):
    Q = 10 ton x 3.516 853 kW/ton = 35.168 53 kW

Route B — NIST W factor (SP 811, App. B.9):
    Q = 10 ton x (3.516 853 E+03 W/ton) = 35 168.53 W = 35.168 53 kW

Route C — from the defining relation and the exact Btu_IT joule equivalent:
    1 Btu_IT = 1 055.05585262 J (exact)
    1 h = 3 600 s
    1 ton = 12 000 Btu_IT/h x 1 055.05585262 J/Btu_IT / 3 600 s/h
          = 3 516.852 842 066 7 W = 3.516 852 842 066 7 kW
    Q = 10 ton x 3.516 852 842 066 7 kW/ton = 35.168 528 420 667 kW

Cross-check of Route C against NIST's rounded Btu_IT/h entry (2.930 711 E-01 W per Btu_IT/h):
    12 000 x 0.293 071 1 = 3 516.853 2 W = 3.516 853 kW/ton — identical to NIST's ton-of-refrigeration entry.

3. ROUNDING TO FOUR SIGNIFICANT FIGURES

Full precision is carried through the multiplication and rounding is applied only to the final result, per the NIST SP 811 procedure (Sec. B.3 and Sec. 7.9, "rounding the converted numerical value"):

    35.168 53 kW  ->  four significant figures  ->  35.17 kW

(The fifth significant figure is 8, so the fourth figure rounds up from 1 to 2: 35.16|853 -> 35.17.)
Using the exact Route C value instead gives 35.168 528... kW -> 35.17 kW. The result is therefore robust: whether the 7-significant-figure NIST table entry or the exact underlying value is carried, the four-significant-figure answer is 35.17 kW. Rounding must not be applied to the per-ton factor first (3.5169 x 10 = 35.169 -> 35.17 kW agrees here, but rounding intermediates is bad practice and can flip the last digit in other cases).

4. WHY THE IT-Btu VARIANT MATTERS AT THE FOURTH SIGNIFICANT FIGURE

NIST publishes several Btu definitions and they are not interchangeable at four significant figures:
    Btu_IT (International Table)  -> 2.930 711 E-01 W per (Btu_IT/h)  -> 10 ton = 35.17 kW   [used here]
    Btu_th (thermochemical)       -> 2.928 751 E-01 W per (Btu_th/h)  -> 10 ton = 35.15 kW   [not used]
    Btu (mean) / 59 degF / 60 degF variants -> further offsets
Because the ton of refrigeration is defined on the IT Btu, only the 3.516 853 kW/ton (SP 811) or 2.930 711 E-01 W per Btu_IT/h entry is admissible. The thermochemical variant would be wrong by about 0.02 kW, i.e. in the fourth significant figure — exactly the digit the answer is required to state.

5. INTERPRETATION (HVAC ENGINEERING NOTE)

35.17 kW is the chiller's rated heat-removal capacity (cooling effect, kW_th), not its electrical input. Electrical draw is capacity divided by COP (or, in US practice, capacity in tons times kW/ton). For reference only, at a typical 0.6 kW/ton the input would be about 6 kW; at COP 3.0 it would be about 11.7 kW. The 10-ton figure is a nameplate nominal rating at rating conditions (e.g., AHRI standard conditions); actual delivered capacity varies with entering/leaving water temperature, condenser conditions and fouling, none of which changes the unit conversion.

6. RECORD / DOCUMENTATION LINES

    Rated cooling capacity: 10 ton of refrigeration (120 000 Btu_IT/h)
    Conversion factor: 3.516 853 kW/ton of refrigeration (NIST SP 811, App. B; NIST SP 1038)
    Capacity: 35.17 kW (35 170 W; 0.03517 MW) — four significant figures

7. ASSUMPTIONS STATED WITH THE NUMBER (not requested as a table; listed so the figure is not misread)
  - The nameplate 10 tons is the IT-Btu ton (12 000 Btu_IT/h), as the request specifies; no thermochemical or mean-Btu interpretation is applied.
  - The 10-ton value is treated as exact for conversion purposes; the four-significant-figure output is a presentation requirement of the request, not a claim about nameplate tolerance.
  - The result is a thermal (heat-removal) capacity; no electrical input power, COP, EER or kW/ton figure is implied by 35.17 kW.

1. WHAT WAS SEARCHED AND WHAT IT RETURNED

Source of record: Microchip DS40002061B, 'ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P Data Sheet Complete', 2020 Microchip Technology Inc., 653 pages.

Full-text search of all 653 pages returned zero occurrences of each of the following tokens: 'Junction-to-Ambient Thermal Resistance', 'RthetaJA' / 'RθJA', 'thetaJA' / 'θJA', 'degC/W', '°C/W'. That table is Section 38.3.6 Thermal Characteristics of the PIC18(L)F26/45/46K40 family — a different Microchip MCU family. It is not the ATmega328P and it is not the 28-pin package. Do not cite it.
  - theta-JA = 60 degC/W for a '28-pin SPDIP package' from the same PIC18 table. Wrong family and wrong package style (SPDIP is a 0.300-inch shrink DIP variant listed for the PIC18F parts); it is not a DS40002061B value for 28P3.

The ambient limits it does print (-55 to +125 C absolute-maximum operating temperature; TA = -40 to +85 C in Section 29; TA = -40 to +105 C in Section 30) are ambient/operating limits, not junction limits, and substituting one for Tj,max would silently change the meaning of the result. Rejected.

(b) PTOT as Vmax x Imax = 6.0 V x 200.0 mA = 1.2 W. The arithmetic is correct, but this is not a datasheet rating. 'Maximum Operating Voltage 6.0 V' and 'DC Current VCC and GND Pins 200.0 mA' are two independent stress limits in an absolute-maximum list whose own notice states that operating at those conditions is not implied and that exposure may cause permanent damage. The datasheet never labels their product as power dissipation, never states that both may be reached simultaneously, and prints no derating curve. 1.2 W is therefore an engineering artifact, not a Microchip specification, and must not be entered in a thermal budget as 'PTOT per datasheet'. Rejected.

Consequence: with neither theta-JA nor Tj,max nor PTOT available from DS40002061B, no honest numeric answer exists for asks 2 and 4 from the specified source. Both are reported as not stated.


4. PROCEDURE TO OBTAIN A DEFENSIBLE theta-JA FOR THE 28-PIN PDIP (for the design record)

Step 1 — Fix the package identity in the design record: 28P3, 28-lead, 0.300 inch wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package; ATmega328P-PU (industrial -40 to +85 C) or ATmega328P-PN. The 32-lead TQFP (32A), 28-pad QFN/MLF (28M1) and 32-pad QFN/MLF (32M1-A) are different packages with different thermal behaviour; do not share a number across them.

Step 2 — Request the package thermal data from Microchip support / the Microchip Packaging Specification (the datasheet itself points to http://www.microchip.com/packaging for current package drawings). Microchip does not publish theta-JA for this legacy Atmel 28P3 package in DS40002061B; the value must come from Microchip's package thermal characterisation data or from measurement. Record the document number and revision of whatever source is used, so the number is traceable.

Step 3 — If no vendor data is available, measure it per JEDEC JESD51-2 (still air) on a JESD51-3 low-effective-thermal-conductivity test board using the temperature-sensitive-parameter method: power the device to a known Pd, wait for thermal equilibrium, read the TSP (on-die diode forward voltage) calibrated against a known temperature, then theta-JA = (Tj - Tamb) / Pd. Report the board type, copper area, ambient, airflow and Pd alongside the number; a theta-JA quoted without its board condition is not comparable to any other theta-JA.

Step 4 — Until a traceable theta-JA exists, run the thermal budget on power and ambient instead of on junction temperature: compute P = VCC x IDD(T, f, V) plus the I/O term, where the datasheet gives the I/O contribution per pin as CL x VCC x f (CL = load capacitance, VCC = operating voltage, f = average switching frequency of the I/O pin), and hold the calculated dissipation to a conservative fraction of the package capability while keeping the ambient inside the specified operating range (-40 to +85 C for the industrial parts). Note that in still air a 28-lead 0.300-inch PDIP is a poor thermal path, so treat any assumption as needing bench verification with a thermocouple on the package top or an infrared scan at worst-case ambient and worst-case firmware load.

Thermal margin is demonstrated by measurement (method, board, conditions) rather than by datasheet limit.' # NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts): what it does and does not require

## 1. Direct answer

**NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7 requires no specific number of attempts, no specific time window, and no specific lockout duration.** All three are organization-defined parameters. The control *mandates the existence of a limit and of an automatic response*, and leaves every numeric value to the implementing organization (recorded in that organization's security plan / control implementation statement, or in an applicable overlay).

| Ask | What AC-7 says | Fixed value in the publication? |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` | **No** |
| 2. Time period in which they occur | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | **No** |
| 3. Lockout duration | Not stated as such. AC-7b's response is a *Selection*; if 'lock the account or node' is chosen, the duration is `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]`; alternatives are lock until released by an administrator, a delay algorithm, administrator notification, or another organization-defined action | **No** |

Any answer of the form "NIST requires N attempts in M minutes with a K-minute lockout" is incorrect. Those numbers come from other frameworks (CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, vendor hardening guides) or from a specific organization's/overlay's parameter values — never from AC-7 itself.

## 2. Control text (Rev. 5, verbatim)

> **AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS**
>
> **Control:**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.
>
> **Discussion:** The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those components. …

Source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (sha256 fc63bcd61715…), corroborated by the AC-7 page at https://nist-sp-800-53-r5.bsafes.com/docs/3-1-access-control/ac-7-unsuccessful-logon-attamps/ and by the 800-53B-derived OSCAL export. The same bracketed placeholders appear in all three, i.e. the baseline document (SP 800-53B) selects the control but does **not** supply the values either.

## 3. The parameter model — where the numbers actually come from

AC-7 uses two parameter types, and an accurate answer must distinguish them:

- **Assignment** (`[Assignment: organization-defined …]`) — the organization must *supply* a value: the attempt count, the counting window, and (if the lock option is selected) the lock duration.
- **Selection** (`[Selection (one or more): …]`) — the organization must *choose* which response(s) apply: temporary lock, administrative lock, delay algorithm, administrator notification, or another action.

Full parameter inventory for AC-7 and its enhancements in Rev. 5:

| Element | Parameter(s) the organization must define |
|---|---|
| AC-7a | number of consecutive invalid logon attempts; time period |
| AC-7b | response selection; lock duration (if locking); delay algorithm (if delaying); other action (if 'other') |
| AC-7(1) | *Withdrawn — incorporated into AC-7.* (No separate parameters.) |
| AC-7(2) Purge/wipe mobile device | mobile devices; purging/wiping requirements and techniques; number of consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts |
| AC-7(3) Biometric attempt limiting | number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts |
| AC-7(4) Alternate authentication factor | alternate authentication factors; number of consecutive invalid logon attempts before alternate factors are allowed; number of attempts permitted via the alternate factors; time period |

So the complete, correct answer to the request is a four-part statement, not a number: *the organization must (i) set a consecutive-failure limit, (ii) set the window over which failures are counted, (iii) select at least one automatic response, and (iv) if locking, set the lock duration.* AC-7 requires the mechanism and the documentation of the values; it does not require particular values.

## 4. Design considerations AC-7 itself raises (useful when choosing the values)

- **Denial of service / lockout-as-attack.** The Discussion explicitly notes that automatic lockouts are *usually temporary* precisely because permanent or long lockouts can be weaponized against legitimate users. A short attempt limit paired with a long or administrative-only lock is a self-inflicted DoS.
- **Counting window semantics.** The time period in AC-7a is the window over which consecutive failures are counted; a window that is too long approximates a permanent lock, too short makes the limit unreachable. Note AC-7 does not itself specify whether a successful logon resets the counter — that is an implementation decision to document (AC-7(2)'s discussion, for the mobile-device case, does state that successful logons reset the count to zero).
- **Alternate path.** AC-7(4) exists to preserve availability: after the limit is hit, alternate authentication factors can be allowed so an inadvertently locked-out user is not fully denied.
- **Local and network logons alike.** The Discussion states the limit applies regardless of whether logon is local or over the network.
- **Related obligations.** A lockout event should be auditable and user-visible; the AC-7 family context and the adjacent previous-logon-notification material make failure counting and notification a documented, observable behaviour rather than a hidden one.

## 5. Version check

- The control text above is Rev. 5 (final 12/10/2020) and is unchanged in the Rev. 5.1 derived OSCAL rendering (identical placeholders).
- The NIST publication page for Rev. 5 (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) lists the controls touched by the 08/27/2025 Release 5.2.0 patch: new SA-15(13), SA-24, SI-02(07); revised SI-07(12); discussion updates to SA-04, SA-05, SA-08, SA-08(14), SI-02, SI-02(05); related-control updates to the -01 controls, AU-02, AU-03, CA-07, IR-04, IR-06, IR-08, SA-15, SI-02, SI-07. **AC-7 is not on that list**, so the AC-7 answer does not change across Rev. 5 / 5.1 / 5.2.0.
- Rev. 4 differs structurally: the automatic-account-lock behaviour was a separate enhancement in Rev. 4 and is marked in Rev. 5 as "(1) UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS / AUTOMATIC ACCOUNT LOCK — [Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]" The parameter-based, no-fixed-values character of the control is the same, however. Cite Rev. 5 text when the question names Rev. 5.

## 6. Defusing the common conflation (important for a compliance answer)

The Tenable audit-reference page for AC-7a lists audit items such as "Set 'Account lockout threshold' to '5 invalid logon attempt(s)'", "Set 'Account lockout duration' to '15 or more minute(s)'" and "Reset account lockout counter after '15 minute(s)'". **These are CIS Benchmark / DISA STIG audit procedures that map to AC-7; they are not NIST requirements.** AC-7 supplies no such figures, and the Tenable page's own AC-7a description reproduces the `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` / `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` placeholders. If a stakeholder "remembers" a NIST number, it is almost certainly one of these, or a FedRAMP/agency overlay value, or the organization's own documented parameter.

## 7. How to state this in a compliance deliverable

1. Quote AC-7 verbatim with the brackets intact — do not fill them in in the control text.
2. Add a parameter table (as in §3) with a "source of value" column pointing to the organization's security plan, the applicable overlay (e.g., a FedRAMP or agency profile), or the system's control implementation statement — whichever actually sets the values for that system.
3. Record the chosen values with justification tied to the DoS/lockout-attack trade-off in the Discussion, and document the counting-window and counter-reset semantics.
4. If an auditor asks for the NIST-mandated number, the correct response is: "AC-7 mandates that a limit, a window, and an automatic response exist and that they be organization-defined; the values are [our documented values], sourced from [our SSP / overlay], not from SP 800-53."

## 8. Note on the not-stated determination

Ask 3 (lockout duration) is recorded in `not_stated`: the harness searched the full text of the Rev. 5 PDF, the 800-53B-derived OSCAL export, the Rev. 5.1 derived OSCAL PDF, the bsafes AC-7 page and the NIST publication page for "lockout duration" and its synonyms, and none occurs — AC-7b says only "lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]", so no duration figure is given here. The proofs of absence recorded for asks 1 and 2 run against the NIST publication *landing* page (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final), which contains no control text at all; they therefore do not show AC-7 to be silent on those points. AC-7 does address both — through organization-defined assignment parameters — so asks 1 and 2 are answered above with the parameter designation rather than reported as unstated or blocked. No ask is blocked: the grounding contains the authoritative control text for every part of the question.

# NASA-STD-4003A, Class R (EMI/RF) bonding — what the standard actually requires

## Bottom line

**NASA-STD-4003A does not specify any maximum RF impedance, in ohms, at any stated frequency, for a Class R bond joint.** The request's premise — that the standard contains an ohm-valued RF impedance ceiling at some frequency — is not supported by the document. Class R is a **performance-based** requirement ("low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest") plus **one numeric limit, and that limit is dc resistance: 2.5 milliohms maximum across each joint in the path.** The standard itself warns that meeting 2.5 mΩ dc does not establish a good RF bond, and that an acceptable RF bond impedance "may be in the ohms range."

Source read: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 (Revalidated 03/13/2026), https://standards.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/standards/NASA/w/CHANGE-1/1/NASA-STD-4003A.pdf (sha256 382567320239) and the revalidated copy (sha256 78283e0027c8); historical NASA-STD-4003 (sha256 a8bd7d04a6bb). The Change 1 revalidation did not alter clause 4.1.4.

## 1. The controlling text — clause 4.1.4, Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)

> "The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.
>
> a. [EBR 20] All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.
>
> b. [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.
>
> (1) [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.
>
> c. [EBR 23] The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle."

Note precisely what EBR 21 does and does not say: it names **inductance, overall impedance, and resonances** as the design quantities, and it states the acceptance criterion **qualitatively** — "low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest." It attaches **no ohm value and no frequency**. The single hard number in the clause is EBR 22, which is explicitly **dc resistance**, **per joint**, **2.5 milliohms**.

## 2. The class-summary table entry for Class R

NASA-STD-4003A's class table carries, in the Class R column:

> "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort."
>
> DC BOND RESISTANCE REQMT.: "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required."
>
> FREQ. REQMT.: High     CURRENT REQMT.: Low

Again: a qualitative RF statement and a 2.5 mΩ dc number. No ohm-at-frequency figure.

## 3. Appendix B.3.4 rationale — the standard's own statement that 2.5 mΩ is not an RF criterion

> "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond."

This is dispositive. The standard explicitly contemplates a joint that passes 2.5 mΩ dc while presenting a high RF impedance, and it does **not** close that gap with a numeric RF limit. It closes it with a design obligation (EBR 21) and an analysis/inspection obligation (section 8, below).

## 4. The historical edition says the same thing even more plainly

Historical NASA-STD-4003 (pre-A), Appendix rationale:

> "The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation (e.g., the chemical formulation used for the conversion coating, and the thickness thereof), the area of the faying surfaces in contact, and the amount of pressure holding the surfaces together."
>
> "The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms."
>
> "Class 'R' bonds should be low impedance at the frequency of interest. Calculations should be made to determine the impedance of any RF bond other than direct metal-to-metal contact over a large surface area."

An acceptable Class R bond with RF impedance "in the ohms range" is stated as normal. There is therefore no basis in any revision of this standard for quoting an ohm-valued RF ceiling, and any such figure a designer has seen came from somewhere else.

## 5. Where the 2.5 mΩ figure applies elsewhere in the standard (all dc)

The same dc limit is repeated for specific Class R sub-paths, which is useful when building a compliance matrix:

- "The dc resistance for each joint in the backshell-to-case path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."
- "The dc resistance of all such joints shall be no greater than 2.5 milliohms."
- "The dc resistance of each such shield termination shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."

All are dc, all are per-joint, none is frequency-referenced.

## 6. Verification the standard requires

- "The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds."
- "Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection."

So compliance for Class R is a **two-legged demonstration**: (i) measured dc resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint on sample/representative bonds, and (ii) **analysis plus inspection** showing the path inductance and impedance, including resonances, are low enough at the frequencies of interest. The second leg is where the engineering judgment lives, because the standard gives no number for it.

Accepted measurement practice for the dc leg (from NASA MSFC connector bonding test, NTRS 20140008725, which applies NASA-STD-4003A): four-probe Kelvin method with a calibrated micro-ohmmeter, acceptance "electrical resistance must not exceed 2.5 mΩ."

## 7. What this means for the designer — how to actually close a Class R bond

Because the requirement is performance-based, the program must **generate** the number rather than look it up. Recommended procedure:

1. **Set the frequencies of interest.** Derive them from the vehicle's emitter/antenna bands, receiver sensitivities, and the MIL-STD-461 test bands used in the EMC control plan. Document them in the bonding control plan; that list *is* the "stated frequency" for your program, not a NASA figure.
2. **Prefer direct metal-to-metal contact.** EBR 20/23 and the class table: "Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort." Maximize faying-surface area and contact pressure; control surface preparation and finish.
3. **If a strap is unavoidable**, keep it short and wide. Companion NASA handbook guidance (NTRS 19970005154, C.2.3.5.3): "A rule of thumb is to use straps with a maximum 5:1 length-to-width ratio." Thin conductor is acceptable at RF because of skin depth, but inductance — not cross-section — is the driver.
4. **Compute Z(f) for the path, not just the joint.** For each path: Z(f) = sqrt(R_dc² + (2πfL)²), with L taken from the actual geometry including height above structure; include resonance effects where the path length approaches a quarter wavelength.
5. **Worked example (engineering illustration, NOT a standard limit).** Copper strap, l = 100 mm, w = 25 mm, t = 0.5 mm:
   - R_dc = ρl/(wt) = (1.72e-8 × 0.10)/(0.025 × 5e-4) = **0.138 mΩ** — passes the 2.5 mΩ per-joint limit with large margin, which is exactly the trap Appendix B.3.4 warns about.
   - Over structure at average height h = 3 mm (w >> h): L ≈ μ0·h·l/w = (1.2566e-6 × 0.003 × 0.10)/0.025 = **15.1 nH**.
   - X at 100 MHz = 2π(1e8)(15.1e-9) = **9.5 Ω**; Z ≈ 9.5 Ω. At 10 MHz: 0.95 Ω. At 1 MHz: 0.095 Ω.
   - Raise the same strap to h = 10 mm and L = 50.3 nH, X at 100 MHz = **31.6 Ω** — a 3.3× penalty for routing it 7 mm further off structure.
   Conclusion the standard intends: at the frequencies of interest the *geometry* sets the impedance, and a joint that measures 0.1 mΩ dc can still be a poor RF bond. This is why EBR 21 is written as a design obligation and verified by analysis and inspection.
6. **Inspect and document.** Photograph and record faying-surface preparation, fastener torque/pressure, strap length-to-width ratio, and standoff height; keep the impedance calculation with the installation drawing.

## 8. Common confusions to avoid (likely sources of the premise)

- **Figure 1, "Maximum Allowable Resistance" curve.** In NASA-STD-4003A this is invoked by the Class H/L hazardous-area clause ("The resistance of bond joints in such areas shall not exceed the Maximum Allowable Resistance curve shown in figure 1"), **not** by Class R. It is not an RF impedance criterion.
- **MIL-B-5087B Class R.** Also a dc resistance criterion (2.5 mΩ), not an ohm-at-frequency RF impedance. NASA-STD-4003A is the successor document and carries the same number.
- **Program-specific or subsystem-specific numbers** (e.g., "≤ 1 Ω at 30 MHz", "≤ 100 mΩ at 1 MHz") that appear in EMC control plans, antenna grounding specs, or launch-site ground support criteria are **contractor or program tailoring**, not NASA-STD-4003A requirements. NASA-STD-4003A explicitly allows such tailoring: "Additional data is provided to support tailoring for new applications, if necessary."
- **Whole-path vs per-joint.** 2.5 mΩ is a **per-joint** dc limit. The RF requirement in EBR 21 applies to the **entire path including resonances**; a chain of joints each at 2.4 mΩ can still be an unacceptable RF path.

## 9. Direct answers

- **Ask 1 (maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency):** none is stated. NASA-STD-4003A contains no ohm-valued RF impedance limit at any frequency for Class R. This is recorded in `not_stated`: the harness searched the full text of https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/NASA/NASA-STD-4003 (7,708 characters, fetched 2026-11-24T23:36:45Z, sha256 fcf6ac58987d) for "RF impedance", "impedance", "ohms", "Class R", "EMI/RF", "bond joint" and "100 mΩ" and found none of them; the document's own Class R clause (4.1.4, EBR 20–23), its class table, and Appendix B.3.4 likewise carry no such figure.
- **Ask 2 (the ohms-at-a-stated-frequency format):** not applicable — there is no such figure in the standard to express in that format. The only numeric Class R bond limit is 2.5 mΩ dc, which is frequency-independent.
- **Ask 3 (what the standard actually requires):** performance-based design of all Class R bond paths and their joints so that inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest (EBR 21); direct metal-to-metal contact preferred with no jumpers, short wide strap only as last resort; dc resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ across each joint in the path (EBR 22); Class R bonding of all outer mold line components to form a uniform low-impedance enclosure (EBR 23); verified by dc resistance testing of sample bonds plus analysis and inspection of the low-inductance path.

CHILLER COOLING CAPACITY — 10 US TONS OF REFRIGERATION TO KILOWATTS (NIST)

ANSWER: 35.17 kW (four significant figures). Unrounded: 35.16853 kW.

1. AUTHORITY AND FACTOR USED
Source: NIST Special Publication 811, 2008 Edition, "Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)" (Thompson & Taylor), conversion-factor table for power. The exact line reads:

  "ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT / h) ...... watt (W) ...... 3.516 853 E+03"

So the official NIST factor is:
  1 ton of refrigeration = 3.516 853 E+03 W = 3.516 853 kW

Two supporting entries in the same table, used below for an independent check:
  "British thermal unitIT per hour (BtuIT / h) ...... watt (W) ...... 2.930 711 E-01"
  "British thermal unitIT per second (BtuIT / s) ...... watt (W) ...... 1.055 056 E+03"
Footnote 9 of the same publication: the Fifth International Conference on the Properties of Steam (London, July 1956) defined the International Table calorie as 4.1868 J exactly; therefore the exact conversion factor for the International Table Btu is 1.055 055 852 62 kJ. The ton of refrigeration is thus exact by definition, with no uncertainty.

2. CALCULATION
Path A — direct, using the NIST ton-of-refrigeration entry:
  Q = 10 ton x 3.516 853 kW/ton = 35.168 53 kW

Path B — from first principles through Btu_IT/h, as an audit check:
  Q = 10 ton x 12 000 Btu_IT/(h·ton) = 120 000 Btu_IT/h
  Q = 120 000 Btu_IT/h x 2.930 711 E-01 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 35 168.53 W = 35.168 53 kW

Path C — from the exact IT Btu definition:
  1 Btu_IT = 1055.055 852 62 J (exact)
  1 h = 3600 s (exact)
  Q = 120 000 x 1055.055 852 62 / 3600 J/s = 35 168.5284 W = 35.168 5284 kW

All three paths agree to better than 0.000 002 kW (2 mW), i.e. far inside the fourth significant figure. The residual difference between Path B and Path C is only the 7-significant-figure rounding of the tabulated 2.930 711 E-01 W per Btu_IT/h; it does not affect the reported result.

3. ROUNDING (ASK 3)
Value to be reported: 35.168 53 kW.
Four significant figures: digits 3-5-1-7 -> 35.17 kW (the fifth digit is 8, so the fourth figure rounds up from 1 to 2).
Round, do not truncate: truncation would give 35.16 kW, which is wrong under the stated four-significant-figure requirement.
Reported as: 35.17 kW.

4. WHY THE Btu DEFINITION MATTERS (documented, not applied)
The request specifies Btu_IT, and the NIST ton-of-refrigeration entry is defined on Btu_IT, so no substitution is made. For traceability, had the thermochemical Btu been used instead (Btu_th/h = 2.928 751 E-01 W):
  Q = 120 000 x 1054.350 / 3600 = 35 145.0 W = 35.145 kW -> 35.14 kW at four significant figures.
That is a 0.02 kW difference, which is exactly the fourth-significant-figure sensitivity the request is guarding against. The IT basis is the correct one here and is the one NIST publishes for the ton of refrigeration.

5. ENGINEERING NOTE ON WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS
35.17 kW is the chiller's COOLING (thermal) capacity — the rate at which it removes heat at its rating point — not its electrical input. Compressor electrical demand would be this value divided by the coefficient of performance (equivalently, capacity in tons multiplied by the kW/ton efficiency figure). A typical water-cooled machine at, say, 0.60 kW/ton would draw about 6.0 kW of electrical power to deliver this 35.17 kW of cooling. The nameplate "10 tons" is a nominal AHRI-basis rating; no altitude, fouling, or part-load derating has been applied, because none applies to a pure unit conversion.

6. CONVERSION CHAIN FOR THE RECORD
  10 ton x 12 000 Btu_IT/(h·ton) = 120 000 Btu_IT/h
  x 1055.055 852 62 J/Btu_IT = 1.266 067 023 E+08 J/h
  / 3600 s/h = 35 168.5284 J/s = 35 168.5284 W
  / 1000 = 35.168 5284 kW
  -> 35.17 kW (4 s.f.)

THERMAL RATING OF THE ATmega328P (28-PIN PDIP) PER DS40002061B — FINDINGS AND THE SUBSTITUTE THERMAL BUDGET A DESIGN MUST CARRY INSTEAD

1. ANSWER

Ask 2 (junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, from DS40002061B): NOT STATED. The document contains no thermal-resistance data for any package.

Ask 5 (maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation specified in DS40002061B): NOT STATED. Neither a TJMAX nor a PTOT is printed.

This is a real absence in the source, not a lookup failure. The full text of DS40002061B (653 pages, 932,316 characters, sha256 b9b9d83cda56, fetched 2026-11-24) was searched for every string a thermal statement is printed with — "RθJA", "Junction-to-Ambient", "Thermal Resistance", "°C/W", "TJA", "RthJA" — and none of them occurs anywhere in the document. The ATMEGA328P product page and the ATmega328P automotive datasheet (Atmel-7810, 294 pages) were searched for the same vocabulary with the same result. There is no page in DS40002061B from which a figure could be read or computed: the document has no partial thermal data (no θJC, no derating curve, no power-vs-temperature table) that could be combined into a θJA.

What the document does contain, so the check can be seen to be fair:
- Section 31 and Section 35, "DC and AC Characteristics Graphs and Tables" (pp. ~505-515 and ~600-610 in the fetched text): per-package typical curves for I/O pin output voltage vs. sink/source current at -40/25/85/105 °C, input threshold voltage vs. VCC, and input hysteresis. Electrical, not thermal.
- Section 39, "Package Drawings" (pp. ~636-641 in the fetched text): mechanical drawings only — 28M1, 32M1-A, and the 32-lead VQFN (Microchip drawing C04-21400). No thermal characteristics table.
- The Electrical Characteristics chapter carries absolute maximum ratings, DC characteristics, speed grades and system/clock specifications. It has no "Thermal Characteristics" section.
This is exactly why the search for "°C/W" over 653 pages returns nothing: Microchip's AVR and PIC datasheets that do publish thermal data print it as a dedicated table with θJA in °C/W per package plus a TJMAX (e.g. PIC18F27/47Q10 Table 39-6: θJA 60 °C/W for the 28-pin SPDIP, TJMAX 150 °C; AVR-DA Table 37-9: θJA 60 °C/W for the 28-pin PDIP (SP), TJMAX "refer to Absolute Maximum Ratings"). The ATmega48A/328 document has no such table.

Consequence for the project: no thermal number in the design file may cite DS40002061B. Any thermal claim must cite a measurement, Microchip's package thermal data, or the explicitly-labelled substitute below.

2. SUBSTITUTE VALUES (NOT FROM DS40002061B — LABEL THEM AS SUCH)

theta_JA = 60 °C/W for the 28-lead PDIP, still air, JEDEC 2s2p board. Basis: Microchip's own thermal tables for 28-pin DIP packages converge on this figure — PIC18F27/47Q10 Table 39-6 gives 60 °C/W for the "28-pin SPDIP package"; AVR-DA Table 37-9 gives 60 °C/W for the "28-pin PDIP package (SP)". Carry a ±30% band (45-80 °C/W) until confirmed, because still-air DIP figures move with board copper and airflow.

Tj_max = 150 °C. This is the TJMAX Microchip prints in the thermal tables of the AVR-DA and PIC18 families. It is an assumption for this part, not a datasheet value.

The limit that IS printed for the ordering code ATmega328P-PU is the operating ambient range, -40 °C to +85 °C. That is an ambient limit, not a junction limit, and does not substitute for the missing TJMAX.

3. POWER BUDGET FROM THE SUBSTITUTES

P_D = VCC × IDD + Σ (VCC - VOH) × IOH + Σ VOL × IOL   (the form Microchip prints in its thermal tables)

Allowable dissipation at theta_JA = 60 °C/W and Tj_max = 150 °C, Pd_max = (150 - Ta)/60:
  Ta = 25 °C -> 2.08 W
  Ta = 40 °C -> 1.83 W
  Ta = 55 °C -> 1.58 W
  Ta = 70 °C -> 1.33 W
  Ta = 85 °C -> 1.08 W
  Ta = 105 °C -> 0.75 W

Actual dissipation for a representative 5 V / 16 MHz design:
  Core: IDD ~ 12 mA typ -> 60 mW.
  I/O: 8 indicator LEDs at 20 mA with VOL = 0.5 V -> 8 × 10 mW = 80 mW.
  Total 140 mW -> self-heating 140 mW × 60 °C/W = 8.4 °C -> Tj = 93.4 °C at Ta = 85 °C. Passes with ~57 °C of margin to 150 °C. At 3.3 V / 8 MHz (~5 mA core, no LEDs) the rise is ~1 °C.

4. THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS CURRENT, NOT theta_JA

The DC absolute maximum ratings cap 40 mA per I/O pin and 200 mA total through VCC/GND. Driving the full 200 mA at 5 V is 1.0 W, which at theta_JA = 60 °C/W gives a 60 °C rise — Tj = 145 °C at Ta = 85 °C, only 5 °C below the assumed 150 °C junction limit, and above it once the ±30% theta_JA band or an enclosure is applied. So at 85 °C ambient the part cannot be run anywhere near its absolute-maximum current. At Ta = 25 °C the same 1.0 W gives Tj = 85 °C, which is comfortable.

Design rule adopted: at Ta <= 85 °C hold total device dissipation <= 0.5 W (50% derating) -> Tj <= 115 °C, 35 °C of margin. At Ta <= 55 °C allow 1.0 W.

5. ENCLOSURE SENSITIVITY (multiply by the enclosure's effective theta_JA)

Dissipation 0.14 W: 60 °C/W -> +8.4 °C; 90 °C/W (vented plastic box) -> +12.6 °C; 120 °C/W (sealed box) -> +16.8 °C.
Dissipation 0.50 W: 60 °C/W -> +30 °C; 90 °C/W -> +45 °C; 120 °C/W -> +60 °C (this last case exceeds the 85 °C ambient design point at Ta > 25 °C — do not put a 0.5 W PDIP design in a sealed box without a measurement).

6. LAYOUT AND PACKAGE RULES FOR THE 28-PIN PDIP

- Solder the PDIP directly to the board. A socket inserts roughly 10-20 °C/W between the leadframe and the PCB copper; a socketed part in a warm enclosure is the single most common way this part overheats.
- The DIP leadframe conducts mainly through its pins, so the high-value copper is the connection from pin 7 (VCC) and pin 8 (GND) into planes on both layers — wider than a 0.25 mm trace, with multiple vias per pin. A top-side pour around the body helps far less than good pin-to-plane conduction.
- Keep the linear regulator, the LED series resistors and any other dissipating part at least 10 mm away and downstream of the airflow; do not share a copper island with the MCU.
- Keep the crystal and load capacitors away from the regulator's heat plume.
- The on-chip temperature sensor (ADC mux channel, ±10 °C accuracy per the automotive datasheet's temperature-sensor section) is adequate for trending, not for thermal protection. If the enclosure is sealed, add a discrete NTC on the board near the MCU.

7. HOW TO CLOSE THE GAP (procedure, in priority order)

a. Ask Microchip for the package thermal data behind microchip.com/packaging for the 28-lead PDIP used by ATmega328P-PU: theta_JA still air and at 1 m/s, theta_JC, and the test board description. This is the only route to a supplier-sourced number.

b. Or measure per JESD51-2A (still air) and JESD51-6 (forced air) on the actual board, and record the board copper area with the result.

c. Or, for an existing enclosure, run the assembly in a chamber at worst-case ambient, measure the package top with a thermocouple, and estimate Tj = Tc + theta_JC × P with theta_JC ~ 31 °C/W (the 28-pin DIP theta_JC Microchip prints in the AVR-DA thermal table). At 140 mW that correction is ~4 °C.

d. Until (a), (b) or (c) is done, use 60 °C/W with the 50% power derating of Section 4 and record the value as an assumption in the design file.

8. REVIEW CHECKLIST

- Every thermal claim in the design file cites a measurement, Microchip package thermal data, or the 60 °C/W substitute explicitly marked as not-from-datasheet.
- DS40002061B is not cited for any thermal number.
- Worst-case ambient in the enclosure is stated and is <= 85 °C for ATmega328P-PU.
- Total dissipation at that ambient is <= 0.5 W, or a measurement backs a higher figure.
- The part is not socketed if the design point is above 0.25 W.

DETERMINATION — NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) requires no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no specific counting time period, and no specific lockout duration. All three are unfilled assignment parameters that the implementing organization must populate. Asked as three 'what value' questions, the answer to each is: the control states none. No figure is reported for asks 1–3 because the standard prints none, and any number that appears in a compliance artifact for AC-7 must be traceable to an organizational decision recorded in the system security plan, not to SP 800-53.

1. THE CONTROL TEXT (verbatim, as fetched)
From https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (sha256 fc63bcd61715) and reproduced identically in the OSCAL-derived PDF (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9), the controls workbook (sha256 6fc1c2414396) and the GitHub wiki mirror (sha256 cd1eb9903e58):

  AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS
  Control:
  a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon
     attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
  b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment:
     organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an
     administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay
     algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined
     action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Three bracketed parameters sit exactly where the three asks point, and every one of them is empty in the published catalog.

2. PARAMETER MAPPING (what the asks correspond to, and what the control states for each)

  Ask 1 — number of consecutive invalid logon attempts
    Location: AC-7a, first parameter.
    Control text: '[Assignment: organization-defined number]'.
    What SP 800-53 states: no value. Assignment parameter, filled by the organization.

  Ask 2 — time period within which the attempts are counted
    Location: AC-7a, second parameter (and repeated in AC-7(4)(b) for alternate-factor attempts).
    Control text: '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
    What SP 800-53 states: no value. Assignment parameter, filled by the organization.

  Ask 3 — lockout duration
    Location: AC-7b, first selection option: 'lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
    Control text: '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
    What SP 800-53 states: no value, and the duration applies only if the organization selects the timed-lock option at all; AC-7b also permits lock-until-administrator-release, a delay algorithm, administrator notification, or another organization-defined action instead of or in addition to a timed lock. There is therefore no duration the control 'requires' even structurally, let alone numerically.

3. WHY THERE IS NO DEFAULT ANYWHERE IN THE PUBLICATION
The catalog carries no fallback values. The control baseline table on https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/ipd/docs/sp800-53r5-draft-baselines-markup.pdf (sha256 bba84ffcac41) lists 'AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts  AC-7  AC-7  AC-7' across the low, moderate and high columns — the control is assigned to all three baselines, and no parameter values travel with the assignment. The parameter values are supplied downstream by the organization (system security plan, overlays, or agency-specific policy). AC-7(1) 'Automatic Account Lock' is marked '[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7]', so there is no separate enhancement carrying lock parameters either. The remaining enhancements are likewise parameterized, not fixed: AC-7(2) purges/wipes a mobile device after '[Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts'; AC-7(3) limits unsuccessful biometric attempts to '[Assignment: organization-defined number]'; AC-7(4)(b) limits alternate-factor attempts to '[Assignment: organization-defined number] ... during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.

4. WHAT THE PAGES DO SAY (so nothing here is mis-cited as a value)
The AC-7 Discussion is guidance, not a requirement, and it too states no figures. It says the limit applies regardless of whether logon is local or network; that 'due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period'; that organizations may use different delay algorithms for different components; that responses may be implemented at the operating system and application levels; and (per the MITRE CTID renderings, sha256 702cdc410ff3 and 47ef8c325aa1) that 'automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted. However, exceptions may be required based on operational mission or need.' Every temporal reference in that discussion is again 'organization-defined'. No sentence anywhere in the fetched corpus supplies a count, a window, or a duration.

5. EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE (per ask; pages searched in full by the harness, with the phrases sought)
  Ask 1 — https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final (22,401 chars, sha256 dbe8a2c6ffe1): none of 'number of consecutive invalid logon attempts', 'consecutive invalid logon attempts', 'invalid logon attempts', 'unsuccessful logon attempts' present. The phrase does occur on the PDF/workbook/wiki pages, but there the value slot is the empty assignment placeholder quoted in section 1 — the occurrence confirms the parameter exists and is unfilled; it does not supply a number.
