answer:
CLASS R (EMI/RF) BONDING PER NASA-STD-4003A - WHAT THE STANDARD DOES AND DOES NOT REQUIRE

=== 1. BOTTOM LINE (answers all three asks) ===

(1) MAXIMUM RF IMPEDANCE IN OHMS: There is none. NASA-STD-4003A specifies no maximum RF impedance, in ohms or any other unit, for a Class R bond joint.

(2) AT A STATED FREQUENCY: There is no stated frequency and no impedance-vs-frequency limit in the standard. The standard's RF-side requirement is qualitative and refers to "the frequencies of interest," which are defined by the program, not by the standard.

(3) WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY REQUIRES: Class R is a low-inductance, low-impedance bond class with exactly ONE numeric limit - a dc resistance of 2.5 milliohms maximum across each joint in the path. The RF requirement is a design/analysis requirement (impedance and resonances low enough to prevent interference), not a measurable ohms-at-a-frequency spec. See Section 2 for verbatim text.

A designer looking for "X ohms at Y MHz" will not find it in this standard, and should not accept a number quoted from memory or a secondary source. The standard itself explains why (Section 3).

=== 2. THE VERBATIM CLASS R REQUIREMENTS (NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, Sec. 4.1.4 and 4.1.4.1) ===

"4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)
The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.

a. [EBR 20] All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.

b. [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.

(1) [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.

c. [EBR 23] The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle."

"4.1.4.1 Electrical Connectors and Shield Termination
a. [EBR 26] Electrical connectors and their backshells that may be used to terminate cable shields shall be installed to provide a low impedance path from the backshell to the equipment case.
b. [EBR 27] The dc resistance for each joint in the backshell-to-case path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."

Related binding requirements:
- Sec. 4.1 [EBR 5]: a bond may serve more than one purpose and shall meet every applicable class. Example given in the standard: equipment powered from the system supply needs Class R (RF) AND Class H (fault current) - low inductance, <= 2.5 milliohms dc for R, plus fault-current contact area for H.
- Sec. 4.1.1 [EBR 6]: assembly drawings shall carry notes stating the applicable class(es). Put "Class R" on the drawing.
- Table 1 (Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes), Class R row: "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort." DC bond resistance requirement: "2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required." Frequency requirement: High. Current requirement: Low.
- Bond strap construction (Class R): "the bonding straps shall be as short as possible. (1) The bond straps shall be flat in cross-section. (2) The bond straps shall have a length-to-width ratio of less than 5 to 1 to minimize the inductance of the strap."
- Definition: "CLASS R - class of bond for radio frequency current."
- EMI test set-up: "the equipment under test (EUT) bonding method to the copper-top test table will be as close as practicable to the flight configuration (i.e., bond strap, surface mating, etc.)." - so the flight bond hardware, not a test-only strap, is what gets exercised in EMI testing.

=== 3. WHY THERE IS NO OHMS-AT-A-FREQUENCY NUMBER (standard's own rationale) ===

From the Class R rationale appendix (A.3.4 in the base issue, B.3.4 in Change 1):

- "There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent. The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation (e.g., the chemical formulation used for the conversion coating, and the thickness thereof), the area of the faying surfaces in contact, and the amount of pressure holding the surfaces together."
- "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond."
- "The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms." (original NASA-STD-4003, same technical content)
- "The electrical bond path between an electronic box and the structure has a complex equivalent circuit that may be simplified to a resistance in series with an inductance all in parallel with a capacitance... At higher frequencies, where the diameter or thickness of the strap significantly exceeds the skin depth, the ac resistance becomes larger than the dc resistance. The ac resistance increases with the square root of frequency."
- "At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit."
- "Isolated structural elements with linear dimensions approaching 1/4 wavelength can pick up and re-radiate RF from high power transmitters or develop enough voltage to produce a glow discharge or arcing to other elements. This should be taken into account when sizing the length of straps or jumpers used for Class R bonds."
- "The Class R bond is not required on all equipment, but it is difficult to determine in advance which equipment really needs to be well bonded. The low impedance to structure is necessary for certain power line to equipment chassis filters and for proper operation of cable shields terminated to equipment chassis."

Read together: the standard deliberately declines to convert an RF impedance requirement into a single number, because the correct value is a function of the interference environment, the geometry, the surface preparation, and the frequency band. Any single "ohms at MHz" figure would be a program-specific derivation, not a standard requirement.

=== 4. WHAT THE DESIGNER SHOULD DO INSTEAD ===

Design rules that flow directly from the requirements (these are the actionable content of EBR 20-23):

1. Direct metal-to-metal contact over the largest practical faying area is the preferred Class R bond. Bond strap = last resort, and then only a short, wide, flat strap.
2. No jumpers, no round wire, no braid with a poor length-to-width ratio.
3. Strap geometry: flat cross-section; length-to-width ratio < 5:1 (hard requirement); as short as possible. Length dominates inductance far more than width (see the worked example - doubling width buys ~23%, halving length buys ~62%).
4. Keep any isolated bond element well under 1/4 wavelength at the highest frequency of interest (at 100 MHz, free-space lambda/4 = 0.75 m; near structure the effective value is lower - keep straps in the few-cm class, not the tens-of-cm class).
5. Bond at multiple points where possible - parallel paths divide inductance and push the parallel resonance upward.
6. Finish compatibility and corrosion control are part of the joint design; the standard's rationale explicitly ties achievable impedance to conversion coating chemistry and thickness, faying area, and contact pressure.
7. Put the class on the drawing (EBR 6).
8. Apply the strictest applicable class when a joint serves multiple purposes (EBR 5).

=== 5. WORKED IMPEDANCE CALCULATION (shows why dc compliance is not RF compliance) ===

Model the bond path as R in series with L, with a shunt C across it (the standard's own simplified equivalent circuit).

Strap: l = 10 cm, w = 2.5 cm, t = 0.5 mm  ->  L/W = 4:1 (satisfies the < 5:1 rule).
Flat-strap inductance (l, w, t in cm):
  L = 2*l*[ ln(2l/(w+t)) + 0.5 + (w+t)/(3l) ] nH
    = 2*10*[ ln(20/2.55) + 0.5 + 2.55/30 ] nH
    = 20*[ 2.060 + 0.5 + 0.085 ] nH
    = 53 nH

Worst-case joint resistance allowed by EBR 22: R = 2.5 mOhm = 0.0025 Ohm.
|Z(f)| = sqrt( R^2 + (2*pi*f*L)^2 ):
  f = 100 kHz : 2*pi*f*L = 0.0333 Ohm  -> |Z| = 33.3 mOhm
  f = 1 MHz   : 0.333 Ohm              -> |Z| = 0.333 Ohm
  f = 10 MHz  : 3.33 Ohm               -> |Z| = 3.33 Ohm
  f = 30 MHz  : 9.99 Ohm               -> |Z| = 9.99 Ohm
  f = 100 MHz : 33.3 Ohm               -> |Z| = 33.3 Ohm (capacitive effects dominate before this)

A joint that passes the 2.5 mOhm dc test by a wide margin is a 3.3 Ohm impedance at 10 MHz and a 10 Ohm impedance at 30 MHz. That is the standard's point, stated numerically.

Resonance: with a shunt capacitance of 100 pF (realistic for a strap routed near structure):
  f_res = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(53e-9 * 100e-12)) = 69 MHz
  Q = 2*pi*f_res*L/R = 9,200
  Z at resonance ~ L/(C*R) = Q^2*R = 53e-9/(100e-12 * 0.0025) = ~212 kOhm
This is the "impedance may rise to thousands of ohms" behavior the standard warns about, and it is why EBR 21 says "including resonances."

Geometry sensitivity (same R, same 10 MHz):
  l = 5 cm, w = 2.5 cm  -> L = 20.3 nH -> |Z| = 1.28 Ohm  (62% reduction for half the length)
  l = 10 cm, w = 5 cm   -> L = 40.9 nH -> |Z| = 2.57 Ohm  (23% reduction for double the width)
Conclusion: shorten first, widen second, and get metal-to-metal contact if at all possible.

=== 6. IF YOUR PROGRAM CONTRACTUALLY NEEDS A NUMBER (tailoring, NOT a standard requirement) ===

NASA-STD-4003A is explicitly written to be tailored (Sec. 1.1: "Additional data is provided to support tailoring for new applications"). If a supplier or a test plan demands "X ohms at Y MHz," derive it and document the derivation:

Step 1 - Define the frequencies of interest. Union of: transmitter bands on the vehicle, receiver bands (including out-of-band susceptibility), the platform's EMI test sweep points (e.g., the CE/RE/RS test frequency ranges your program invokes), and any known resonant frequencies of cable/box/structure geometries. Write this list into the bonding control document - it is what EBR 21 means by "frequencies of interest."

Step 2 - Define the allowable voltage across the joint. From the interference budget: receiver sensitivity degradation, shield termination voltage, filter performance, or an emissions limit with margin.

Step 3 - Compute Z_allow = V_allow / I_worst-case.
  Worked example: worst-case common-mode RF current on a shield at 30 MHz = 20 mA; allowable shield-to-chassis voltage to preserve the emissions margin = 1.0 V. Then Z_allow = 1.0 V / 0.020 A = 50 Ohm at 30 MHz.
  Check against the design: the 53 nH strap above gives 9.99 Ohm at 30 MHz, which is under the 50 Ohm derived budget - design is compliant.

Step 4 - Allocate the budget across the joints and the strap (e.g., 50% to the strap, 25% per joint), then verify by analysis. Document that this limit is a program-derived requirement satisfying EBR 21, not a NASA-STD-4003A numeric requirement.

=== 7. VERIFICATION / COMPLIANCE APPROACH ===

- DC resistance: measure each joint in the path against 2.5 mOhm (EBR 22), and each backshell-to-case joint against 2.5 mOhm (EBR 27). Four-wire (Kelvin) measurement with clean probe placement on the faying surfaces; record test current and probe separation in the procedure (the standard does not prescribe the instrument; your program's metrology procedure does - do not quote a test current as if it came from 4003A).
- Low inductance / RF impedance: the standard's mechanism for this class is analysis and inspection of the configuration, not an RF impedance measurement. The requirement is that the design be shown low enough at the frequencies of interest - so the deliverable is an impedance-vs-frequency analysis (as in Section 5) plus inspection of strap geometry (flat, L/W < 5:1, short, no jumpers, direct contact where required, resonance check against the frequency list).
- Similarity and process control: sample bonds of the same type and process are tested, and other bonds verified by similarity, with spot checks to confirm the process has not drifted.
- EMI test: the EUT-to-ground-plane bond in EMI testing must replicate the flight configuration (bond strap, surface mating), so an unrealistic test bond will hide or create problems.

=== 8. PROVENANCE, REVISION, AND CAVEATS ===

- Governing text quoted above is from NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 (revalidated copy, 47 pp.) and is identical in the base NASA-STD-4003A (35 pp.); requirement numbers EBR 20-23 and EBR 26-27 are the Change 1 tagging.
- NASA-STD-4003 (the predecessor) carried the same technical content with different numbering (Sec. 4.3) and additionally stated the equipment-case-to-structure and mounting-plate 2.5 mOhm limits as separate sentences.
- CONFIRM THE GOVERNING REVISION against your contract. The question names 4003A; if your program is on a later revision or a program-specific bonding spec (or a prime's bonding document), the class definitions and numbering may differ even where the physics does not. Nothing in this answer should be substituted for the controlled copy of the document your contract cites.
- Do not carry the 2.5 mOhm figure into an RF budget as if it were an RF impedance. The standard says the opposite in plain language.
- The only number from this standard that belongs in a Class R requirement flowdown is: 2.5 milliohms dc maximum per joint (and per backshell-to-case joint), with a low-inductance geometry requirement that must be verified by analysis and inspection against a program-defined list of frequencies of interest.

CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 TON OF REFRIGERATION TO kW (NIST)

1. SOURCE OF THE CONVERSION FACTOR (ask 1)

NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI), Appendix B.8 (factors listed alphabetically) and Appendix B.9 (factors by kind of quantity, under "Heat Flow Rate"), both carry the entry:

    ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h)  ->  watt (W)  ->  3.516 853 E+03

NIST Special Publication 1038, The International System of Units (SI) - Conversion Factors for General Use, Section 5.2.13 (Power), Table entry:

    ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)  ->  kilowatt (kW)  ->  3.516 853

So the official NIST factor is:

    1 ton of refrigeration (TR) = 3.516 853 kW  (exactly, to the digits NIST publishes; 7 significant figures)

The definition behind the factor is the one stated in the request: 1 TR = 12 000 Btu_IT per hour, where Btu_IT is the International Table British thermal unit.

2. INDEPENDENT RE-DERIVATION OF THE FACTOR (verification, not a substitute source)

From NIST's own component factors in the same appendix:
    Btu_IT = 1.055 056 E+03 J                (Appendix B.9)
    1 h    = 3 600 s

    12 000 Btu_IT/h = 12 000 x 1055.056 J / 3600 s = 12 660 672 / 3600 = 3 516.853 W = 3.516 853 kW   (exact match)

Cross-check via the heat-flow-rate factor:
    Btu_IT/h -> W = 2.930 711 E-01
    12 000 x 0.293 071 1 = 3 516.853 W = 3.516 853 kW   (exact match)

3. THE CONVERSION (ask 2)

    P[kW] = TR x 3.516 853
    P[kW] = 10 x 3.516 853 = 35.168 53 kW

Equivalent working (for a checking engineer who prefers Btu first):
    10 TR x 12 000 Btu_IT/h/TR = 120 000 Btu_IT/h
    120 000 x 0.293 071 1 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 35 168.53 W = 35.168 53 kW

4. ROUNDING TO FOUR SIGNIFICANT FIGURES (ask 3)

    35.168 53 kW -> significant digits are 3, 5, 1, 6 | next digit 8 -> round the 6 up to 7

    ANSWER:  35.17 kW  (four significant figures)

Robustness check on the rounding: the commonly quoted variant of the multiplier, 3.516 8528 kW/TR, gives 10 x 3.516 8528 = 35.168 528 kW, which also rounds to 35.17 kW. The four-significant-figure answer is therefore stable against the last-digit differences between NIST's published multipliers; no ambiguity is introduced by the rounding.

Also state it in the other unit for completeness:
    Q = 10 x 12 000 = 120 000 Btu_IT/h

5. ENGINEERING NOTES ON USE OF THE NUMBER (HVAC interpretation)

- 35.17 kW is the chiller's NOMINAL COOLING CAPACITY (heat rejection rate from the chilled water) at the nameplate rating conditions. It is not the compressor/electrical input power. Input power = capacity / COP (or capacity / EER in mixed units); e.g. at COP 3.0 the electrical draw would be about 11.7 kW, at COP 2.6 about 13.5 kW. Do not use 35.17 kW as an electrical load for cable or breaker sizing.
- The nameplate tonnage is a rating at specific leaving chilled-water temperature, entering condenser water/ambient temperature and flow. Actual delivered capacity at site conditions will differ; for a like-for-like replacement, verify duty from measured flow and temperature difference: Q[kW] = 4.19 x flow[l/s] x dT[K] (water, ~4.19 kJ/kg·K), or in US units Q[Btu/h] = 500 x gpm x dT[°F].
- The ton of refrigeration is a rate of heat transfer, unrelated to the mass of refrigerant in the machine or to tonnes of CO2 equivalent under F-gas rules.

6. FINAL STATEMENT

A 10-ton-of-refrigeration chiller, converted with the NIST-published factor of 3.516 853 kW per ton of refrigeration (1 TR = 12 000 Btu_IT/h), has a nominal cooling capacity of 35.168 53 kW, which is 35.17 kW to four significant figures.

## Answers

**Ask 2 — junction-to-ambient thermal resistance (θJA), ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP (package code 28P3), per DS40002061B:** NOT STATED. The datasheet specifies no θJA for this or any package. No value is returned.

**Ask 3 — maximum junction temperature (TJMAX) or total power dissipation (PTOT), per DS40002061B:** NOT STATED. The datasheet specifies neither a maximum junction temperature nor a total power dissipation rating. No value is returned.

Neither quantity can be computed from figures the datasheet does state, so no derived substitute is offered either. This is a genuine gap in the document, not a lookup failure.

## What was searched, and where

- **Ask 2:** full text of the Microchip ATmega328 product page, https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/ATmega328 (297,140 characters, fetched 2026-11-25T00:06:52Z, sha256 37d543584073), searched for `Junction-to-Ambient Thermal Resistance`, `RθJA`, `θJA`, `°C/W`, `28-pin PDIP`, `PDIP`, `ATmega328P`. **None present.**
- **Ask 3:** full text of Microchip DS80000855C, the ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P Silicon Errata and Data Sheet Clarifications, https://www.farnell.com/datasheets/4320059.pdf (23 pages, 33,156 characters, fetched 2026-11-25T00:06:50Z, sha256 c966775d8934), searched for `Maximum Junction Temperature`, `TJMAX`, `Total Power Dissipation`, `PTOT`, `mW`. **None present.**
- The datasheet passages actually returned by the harness cover only: I/O-pin output-voltage and input-threshold curves (Figures 31-353…31-358, pp. 513–515; Figures 35-22…35-27, pp. 608–610), the 28P3/32A/28M1/32M1-A package drawings (pp. 637–641), packaging/ordering information (p. 627), pin descriptions, and the feature list. There is no thermal-characteristics section among them.

## Why no figure can be derived from the stated parts

θJA is a measured, board-condition-dependent package property (JEDEC JESD51-2/-3/-7). It is not a product, sum or power of any electrical figure the datasheet prints. TJMAX and PTOT likewise appear nowhere as components of another stated number. The only temperatures in the returned passages are:

- I/O-pin characterization temperatures 105 °C, 85 °C, 25 °C, −40 °C (curve families in Figures 31-353…358 and 35-22…27); and
- the operating temperature range −40 °C to +85 °C from the feature list.

None of these is a junction-temperature limit, none is a power rating, and none combines into a thermal resistance. So the correct handling is 'the datasheet states none', not a computed value.

## What the datasheet does contain on this subject

The electrical-characteristics chapter of DS40002061B opens with an Absolute Maximum Ratings block: voltages on pins and on RESET, maximum operating voltage, DC current per I/O pin, DC current on VCC and GND, and the operating/storage temperature ranges. That is a destruction-limit stress table, not a thermal model — it carries no θJA, no TJMAX and no PTOT. The package chapter (Section 39) is mechanical only: body dimensions, lead pitch, seating plane, coplanarity. Confirm this directly at the Absolute Maximum Ratings table in Section 29 of DS40002061B when reviewing; it is the only place in the document where a temperature limit of any kind is printed.

## Consequence for the project, and what to do instead

A thermal budget for this part **cannot be closed from the datasheet alone.** Proceed as follows:

1. **Obtain θJA for the 28P3 package from a source that actually publishes it** — Microchip's Packaging Specification / package thermal data (linked from the datasheet package pages as http://www.microchip.com/packaging), a JESD51-2/-3/-7 report, or your own measurement. Record the source, the test board condition (JEDEC 1s/2s2p) and the airflow. A JEDEC 2s2p number is not the θJA of your board; derating or measurement on the real assembly is required for anything close to the limit.
2. **Adopt a design TJMAX as a project decision, not a datasheet figure.** For a plastic industrial-grade part a common self-imposed limit is 125 °C junction; if you want margin against the −40 to +85 °C ambient range the part is characterized over, use 105 °C or lower. Write the chosen number and its justification into the design record — it must not be attributed to DS40002061B.
3. **Compute dissipation** as P = VCC · ICC(f, VCC, mode) + Σ_pins (VOL · IOL) + Σ_pins ((VCC − VOH) · IOH) + P_ADC + P_peripherals, using the ICC-versus-frequency curves and the I/O VOL/IOH curves at the actual operating temperature.
4. **Check** TA_max + P · θJA ≤ TJMAX with the θJA from step 1. If it fails, reduce clock frequency or VCC, reduce sink/source current per pin, add copper/thermal relief on the PDIP pads, or move to the 32-lead TQFP (32A) which has a far lower θJA than a 0.300" PDIP.
5. **Record the gap** in the component qualification note: 'DS40002061B specifies no θJA, TJMAX or PTOT; thermal margin established from <external source> at <conditions>.'

## Attribution caution

Thermal-resistance numbers for the 28-pin PDIP circulate in distributor parameter tables, third-party thermal databases and application notes. None of them is DS40002061B.
